label: Problem set 4
title: Problem set 4: Absorption, emission and scattering
summary: Practice Lesson 4: how atoms absorb and emit photons of definite energy, why every element has its own line spectrum, and the difference between elastic Rayleigh scattering and inelastic Raman scattering.

intro.text: This set is about what happens when light meets matter. Atoms and molecules have fixed energy gaps, so they absorb and emit only photons whose energy matches a gap exactly. That is the origin of line spectra.
For the calculations, the same photon equation, ΔE = hf = hc/λ, does all the work. Remember that a transition either absorbs or emits one photon of energy equal to the gap.

sections.title: Transitions, spectra and scattering
sections.summary: Connect energy gaps to absorbed and emitted photons, and tell elastic from inelastic scattering.
keyPoints: A photon is absorbed or emitted only when its energy matches a gap between levels.
Line spectra are fingerprints of the elements because the gaps are fixed.
Emission and absorption of the same element occur at the same wavelengths.
Rayleigh scattering is elastic (same energy); Raman scattering is inelastic (shifted).

blocks.text: Think of the energy levels as a staircase. An electron can stand only on a step, never between steps. A photon with exactly the energy of one step can lift the electron up; when the electron falls back down, a photon of the same energy is given out.

blocks.caption: The energy of an absorbed or emitted photon

blocks.text: Because the steps are different for every element, so is the set of photon energies each element can exchange. That is why a line spectrum identifies the element it came from, much as a fingerprint identifies a person.

blocks.title: The wavelength and colour of an absorbed photon
blocks.given: An atom has a transition of energy 3.0 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. Find the wavelength of the light it absorbs. Take hc = 1.99 × 10⁻²⁵ J m.
steps: Convert to nanometres: 6.6 × 10⁻⁷ m = 660 nm, which is red.
blocks.result: The atom absorbs red light of about 660 nm.

blocks.title: Absorption lines
blocks.body: If white light passes through a gas, the gas removes the wavelengths its atoms can absorb. The result is a bright background crossed by dark absorption lines at exactly the wavelengths the gas would emit.

questions.question: Why does each element have its own characteristic line spectrum?
options: the energy-level gaps differ from element to element
electrons are the same in every atom
questions.explanation: The pattern of energy levels is unique to each element, so the photons it can absorb or emit have a unique set of energies. That set of wavelengths is the line spectrum.

questions.question: A substance that absorbs red light looks blue-green (cyan).
questions.explanation: If red is removed from white light, the light that remains to reach your eye is the complementary colour, blue-green. That is why many red-absorbing dyes look cyan.

questions.question: A photon of wavelength 500 nm is emitted. Find its energy, in joules. Take h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J s and c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s.
Find the energy, in joules, of an emitted photon of wavelength 700 nm. Take hc = 1.99 × 10⁻²⁵ J m.
questions.explanation: E = hc / λ = (1.99 × 10⁻²⁵) / (7.0 × 10⁻⁷) = 2.84 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. Red photons are less energetic than blue ones.

questions.question: Which transition emits the most energetic photon (largest energy gap)?
questions.explanation: The gap between n = 1 and n = 2 is the largest, so that transition releases the most energy. In hydrogen it gives an ultraviolet photon.

questions.question: In absorption, an electron moves to a higher energy level.
questions.explanation: The atom gains the photon's energy, so the electron moves up. Emission is the reverse: the electron falls and the atom loses energy as a photon.

questions.question: Which of these are ways in which light interacts with matter? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Absorption, emission and scattering all involve light and matter. Sublimation is a change of state of a solid, nothing to do with the interaction of light with matter.

questions.question: Rayleigh scattering of light by air molecules is:
options: elastic, so the light keeps its energy
inelastic, so the light changes colour
questions.explanation: In Rayleigh scattering the molecule re-emits a photon of the same energy, so the colour is unchanged. Raman scattering is the inelastic case, where a vibration shifts the energy.

questions.question: A molecule has an energy gap of 4.0 × 10⁻²⁰ J. Find the frequency of the photon it absorbs, in hertz. Take h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J s.
questions.explanation: f = ΔE / h = (4.0 × 10⁻²⁰) / (6.626 × 10⁻³⁴) = 6.0 × 10¹³ Hz, in the far infrared.

questions.question: Why does the sky look red at sunset?
options: sunlight travels a longer path through the air, so more blue light is scattered out
questions.explanation: At sunset light crosses much more atmosphere. Short wavelengths are scattered away, leaving the longer red wavelengths to reach your eye directly.

questions.question: The emission and absorption lines of a given element occur at the same wavelengths.
questions.explanation: Both come from the same set of energy gaps. A gap can be crossed either way, so the element absorbs and emits at the same wavelengths.

questions.question: The energy of a photon emitted in a transition equals:
options: the sum of the two energy levels
the difference between the two energy levels
the product of the two levels
questions.explanation: The photon carries away exactly the energy lost by the atom, which is the difference between the upper and lower levels. That is why each transition gives one definite wavelength.

questions.question: A sample transmits 10% of the incident light. Find its absorbance, A = −log₁₀(T), with T = 0.10.
The colour of a solution depends on the wavelengths it absorbs.
questions.explanation: What we see is the transmitted light that remains after absorption, so the absorbed wavelengths set the observed colour.

questions.question: Which processes can remove light from a transmitted beam? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Absorption, scattering and reflection all take light out of the forward beam. Emission would add light, not remove it.
